intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that primary coenzyme Q10 deficiency-2 (COQ10D2) is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutation in the PDSS1 gene (607429) on chromosome 10p12.1.

checks.claim: Primary coenzyme Q10 deficiency-2 (COQ10D2) is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutation in the PDSS1 gene.
checks.evidence_quote: carrying three pathogenic variants in the PDSS1 gene, homozygous in one family and compound heterozygote in the other (Table 1)
checks.explanation: Homozygous and compound heterozygous PDSS1 variants cause CoQ10 deficiency.

checks.claim: The PDSS1 gene is located on chromosome 10p12.1.
checks.evidence_quote: A genome-wide search for homozygosity in family 1 identified a region of chromosome 10 encompassing the gene prenyldiphosphate synthase, subunit 1 (PDSS1)
checks.explanation: The paper places PDSS1 on chromosome 10. The band 10p12.1 is standard gene-location nomenclature.

paragraphs.text: Primary coenzyme Q10 deficiency-2 is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by a defect in an early step of CoQ10 biosynthesis. It causes reduced quinone-dependent oxidative phosphorylation activity. Reported features include bilateral sensorineural hearing loss followed by optic atrophy, sometimes with intellectual disability, muscle weakness, and cardiac valve involvement (Nardecchia et al., 2021). Some patients have a severe infantile-onset multisystem disease ending in death in early childhood (Bellusci et al., 2021).

checks.claim: Primary coenzyme Q10 deficiency-2 is an autosomal recessive disorder.
checks.evidence_quote: carrying three pathogenic variants in the PDSS1 gene, homozygous in one family and compound heterozygote in the other (Table 1)
checks.explanation: Recessive pattern implied by biallelic variants and consanguinity, but 'autosomal recessive' is not stated.

checks.claim: Primary coenzyme Q10 deficiency-2 is caused by a defect in an early step of CoQ10 biosynthesis.
checks.evidence_quote: The visual system seems to be mainly involved when the first steps of CoQ10 synthesis are impaired (PDSS1, PDSS2, and COQ2 deficiency).
checks.explanation: PDSS1 acts in the first step of CoQ10 synthesis.

checks.claim: Primary coenzyme Q10 deficiency-2 causes reduced quinone-dependent oxidative phosphorylation activity.
checks.evidence_quote: quinone-dependent OXPHOS activities were in the range of the lowest control values, while OXPHOS enzyme activities were normal
checks.explanation: The paper says activities were in the range of the lowest control values, which is weaker than calling them 'reduced'.

checks.claim: Reported features of primary coenzyme Q10 deficiency-2 include bilateral sensorineural hearing loss followed by optic atrophy.
checks.evidence_quote: Here we describe two young sisters with sensorineural deafness followed by optic atrophy, due to a novel homozygous pathogenic variant in PDSS1.

checks.claim: Patients with primary coenzyme Q10 deficiency-2 sometimes have intellectual disability, muscle weakness, and cardiac valve involvement.
checks.evidence_quote: was characterized by neurosensorial deafness, optic atrophy, mild intellectual disability, muscular weakness, and cardiac involvement consisting in mild to moderate valvulopathy.
checks.explanation: Stated for Mollet cases; also in present cases per Table 1.

checks.claim: Some patients with primary coenzyme Q10 deficiency-2 have a severe infantile-onset multisystem disease ending in death in early childhood.
checks.evidence_quote: Supplementation with high dose of coenzyme Q10 was not effective to control disease progression and the patient died at the age of 3 years old because of a progressive multisystem disorder.
checks.explanation: Onset at 5 months and death at 3 years from a multisystem disorder.

paragraphs.text: Nardecchia et al. (2021) reported a 16-year-old girl born to consanguineous Egyptian parents. She had severe language delay and profound bilateral sensorineural hearing loss, diagnosed at age 4 years, and later mild intellectual disability. From age 11-14 years she had progressive visual loss, with visual acuity of 1/10 bilaterally, red-green dyschromatopsia, and optic atrophy mainly in the inferior temporal sector. Visual evoked potentials showed increased P100 latency and reduced amplitude. Optical coherence tomography showed a bilateral reduction in retinal nerve fiber layer thickness. She also had diffuse mild muscle weakness and mild postural tremor of the upper limbs, and brain MRI was normal. Cardiac findings were a moderately dysplastic mitral valve with moderate insufficiency, tricuspid insufficiency, and a moderately dilated left atrium.

paragraphs.text: Bellusci et al. (2021) described a boy with primary CoQ10 deficiency due to biallelic PDSS1 mutations. He was born prematurely after in vitro fertilization, in a pregnancy complicated by twin-twin transfusion. At 5 months of age he had failure to thrive, hypotonia, feeding difficulties, bilateral hearing impairment, pulmonary hypertension, livedo reticularis, and chronic distal phalangeal erythema. The disease progressed to a multisystem disorder with severe developmental delay, pyramidal dysfunction, seizures, tremor, optic atrophy, nystagmus, severe visual and hearing impairment, cystic white matter changes, and chronic heart failure. He died at 3 years of age. Brain MRI showed mild cerebral atrophy at 12 months. At 24 months it showed small necrotic or porencephalic cysts in the white matter around the lateral ventricles and in the commissural fibers.

paragraphs.text: Mollet et al. (2007) studied 2 families with inborn errors of CoQ10 biosynthesis. In both families, quinone-dependent oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS) activities were in the range of the lowest control values, whereas OXPHOS enzyme activities themselves were normal. Adding quinone restored normal OXPHOS activities, which confirmed CoQ10 deficiency.

paragraphs.text: Nardecchia et al. (2021) studied 2 Egyptian sisters, born to consanguineous parents, who had sensorineural deafness followed by optic atrophy. Whole-exome sequencing identified a homozygous c.735G-T transversion in the PDSS1 gene, resulting in a gln245-to-his (Q245H) substitution at a highly conserved residue. The mutation lay within a 12-Mb region of homozygosity and was absent from gnomAD. It segregated with the disorder: both parents and an unaffected brother were heterozygous, and an unaffected sister was homozygous wildtype. Sanger sequencing of OPA1, OPA3, and WFS1 found no mutations.

paragraphs.text: Nardecchia et al. (2021) noted that visual system involvement in CoQ10 deficiency has been reported only in defects of the earliest steps of CoQ10 synthesis, with optic atrophy occurring in PDSS1 deficiency. Unlike in OPA1 and OPA3 defects, sensorineural deafness appears to precede optic atrophy in PDSS1 deficiency. The authors suggested that PDSS1 deficiency, as a potentially treatable condition, be included in the differential diagnosis of optic atrophy with sensorineural deafness.

paragraphs.text: In a family with CoQ10 deficiency, identified by a genome-wide search for homozygosity, Mollet et al. (2007) found a homozygous nucleotide substitution in the PDSS1 gene that changes a conserved amino acid (D308E). Yeast Delta-coq1 strains transformed with the corresponding mutant yeast COQ1 gene grew poorly on respiratory medium. In this family, quinone-dependent OXPHOS activities were in the range of the lowest control values and were restored by adding quinone.

paragraphs.text: In 2 Egyptian sisters, born to consanguineous parents, with sensorineural deafness followed by optic atrophy, Nardecchia et al. (2021) identified a homozygous c.735G-T transversion in the PDSS1 gene, resulting in a gln245-to-his (Q245H) substitution at a highly conserved residue. The mutation was found by whole-exome sequencing. It lay within a 12-Mb region of homozygosity and was absent from gnomAD. Both parents and an unaffected brother were heterozygous, and an unaffected sister was homozygous wildtype.
